article.audioae.title: Audio autoencoder on mel spectrograms
article.audioae.subtitle: Self-supervised audio representation project: signal preprocessing, log-mel spectrogram conversion, convolutional autoencoder training, and approximate audio reconstruction.
article.audioae.overview.title: Project goal
article.audioae.overview.text: Learn a compact representation of audio signals without labels by training an autoencoder to reconstruct mel spectrograms. This project shows how to go from a raw audio signal to a time-frequency representation usable by a convolutional network, and then how to evaluate reconstruction quality both visually and through listening.
article.audioae.dataset.title: Data and preprocessing
article.audioae.dataset.text: The project uses the TinySOL dataset, which contains short monophonic recordings of isolated instruments. Each sample is resampled to 16 kHz, adjusted to a fixed duration of one second, and amplitude-normalized in order to obtain consistent inputs and make training more stable.
article.audioae.preprocessing.text: Each waveform is converted into a mel spectrogram using an STFT, then compressed on a logarithmic scale. This step makes the representation more compact, more numerically stable, and highlights frequencies that are more useful for learning.
article.audioae.representation.title: Representation: log-mel spectrograms
article.audioae.representation.text: Using log-mel spectrograms makes it possible to transform a 1D audio signal into a structured 2D representation adapted to convolutional networks. Compared to raw waveforms, this representation is easier to model, easier to read visually, and much faster to train on.
article.audioae.model.title: Model
article.audioae.model.text: The model is a 2D convolutional autoencoder applied to log-mel spectrograms. The encoder is composed of convolution layers followed by normalization and pooling layers, progressively reducing spatial dimensions while increasing the number of channels. This step extracts increasingly abstract features from the audio signal. The spectrogram is then projected into a low-dimensional latent space through a linear layer, forcing the model to compress the essential information. The decoder performs the inverse operation using transposed convolutions, progressively reconstructing a spectrogram with the same dimensions as the input. Training relies on a reconstruction loss, allowing the model to learn a compact and structured representation of the signal without supervision.
article.audioae.training.title: Training
article.audioae.training.text: Training is performed on the full dataset using a reconstruction loss combining MSE and L1 in order to balance optimization stability and detail preservation. The spectrogram dimensions are chosen to remain compatible with the network’s downsampling and upsampling operations, allowing coherent reconstruction at the output.
article.audioae.inference.title: Evaluation
article.audioae.inference.text:
During inference, a validation spectrogram is passed through the autoencoder and then compared to its reconstruction.

The evaluation is first done visually by comparing the overall structure of the spectrograms: the main harmonics and temporal evolution of the signal are reproduced correctly, indicating that the model has captured the dominant audio features. However, some differences appear in low-intensity regions (purple areas on the spectrograms) and in finer details, reflecting information loss caused by compression in the latent space.

An absolute error map is also computed by taking the absolute difference between the original and reconstructed spectrogram at each point. This visualization highlights the areas where reconstruction is the least accurate.

Finally, a listening evaluation is performed by reconstructing an approximate waveform using InverseMelScale and Griffin-Lim. The resulting audio remains degraded, mainly because phase information is not present in the spectrogram.
article.audioae.results.title: Results
article.audioae.results.text: The model succeeds in reconstructing the overall harmonic structure of the samples, with reconstructed spectrograms that remain visually close to the inputs. The reconstructed audio version is noticeably more degraded than the spectrogram itself, highlighting the difficulty of converting a mel spectrogram back into a waveform.
article.audioae.conclusion.title: Conclusion and future work
article.audioae.conclusion.text:
This project illustrates the ability of convolutional autoencoders to learn compact representations of audio signals from spectrograms. The model efficiently captures the overall structure of the signal while also showing its limitations on fine details and audio reconstruction, especially due to the absence of phase information.

Possible improvements include better spectral resolution, the use of variants such as variational autoencoders, or the integration of neural vocoders to improve reconstructed audio quality. Exploring the latent space also opens interesting possibilities for audio signal manipulation and comparison.
